cls: Rapid-acting human insulin analog (recombinant, mealtime/bolus insulin)
pharm: A recombinant human insulin analog in which asparagine at position B3 is replaced by lysine and lysine at B29 is replaced by glutamic acid; these substitutions reduce self-association so it is absorbed rapidly and acts quickly to lower blood glucose by promoting cellular glucose uptake (skeletal muscle, fat) and inhibiting hepatic glucose output.
quick: Individualized; given subcutaneously within 15 min before or within 20 min after starting a meal
Dose with meals; take 0-15 min before or within 20 min after starting eating
Insulin is preferred for glycemic control in pregnancy; individualize and monitor closely
Compatible; insulin is not absorbed orally by the infant - may need to adjust dose/diet
No fixed adjustment; insulin requirements often fall - monitor and titrate
No fixed adjustment; insulin requirements may fall - monitor and titrate
May cause hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia; monitor glucose, caution patients
Blood glucose, HbA1c, potassium, signs of hypo/hyperglycemia, injection sites
summary: Insulin glulisine is a rapid-acting recombinant human insulin analog used to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients (age 4 years and older) with diabetes mellitus. It has a faster onset and shorter duration of action than regular human insulin, making it suitable for mealtime (prandial/bolus) coverage. It should be used with a longer-acting (basal) insulin or basal insulin regimen, except when given by continuous subcutaneous infusion (insulin pump). It is administered within 15 minutes before or within 20 minutes after starting a meal. The principal and most serious adverse effect is hypoglycemia. Doses are individualized based on metabolic needs, blood glucose monitoring, and glycemic goals.
indications: To improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 4 years and older with diabetes mellitus

dosage.d: Individualized dose injected within 15 minutes before a meal or within 20 minutes after starting a meal
dosage.n: Use in regimens that include an intermediate- or long-acting (basal) insulin or basal insulin analog

dosage.d: Individualized; deliver as basal rate plus mealtime bolus per pump system instructions
dosage.n: Change infusion sets and reservoir/glulisine in the reservoir at least every 48 hours; do not dilute or mix with other insulins in the pump

dosage.d: Use at concentrations of 0.05-1 unit/mL in 0.9% sodium chloride
dosage.t: Continuous infusion in a clinical setting
dosage.n: IV use requires close glucose and potassium monitoring; do not give IV outside supervised settings

dosage.d: Starting dose and titration individualized to metabolic needs, blood glucose values, and glycemic goals
dosage.n: Adjust with changes in physical activity, meal patterns, renal/hepatic function, or other insulins

admin: Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm; rotate sites within a region to reduce lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis
Give within 15 minutes before a meal or within 20 minutes after starting the meal
Inspect visually before use - use only if clear and colorless; do not use if cloudy, discolored, or containing particles
When mixed in a syringe, only mix with NPH insulin and draw glulisine into the syringe first; inject immediately after mixing - do not mix with other insulins for subcutaneous injection
For pump use, do not mix or dilute glulisine in the pump; replace reservoir and infusion set per device instructions and at least every 48 hours
Do not share pens, cartridges, or needles between patients even if the needle is changed (risk of bloodborne pathogen transmission)
Never share an insulin pen between patients
moa: Insulin glulisine regulates glucose metabolism by binding to insulin receptors on muscle and fat cells, facilitating cellular uptake of glucose, and by inhibiting glucose production by the liver. Insulin also inhibits lipolysis and proteolysis and enhances protein synthesis. The amino acid substitutions (asparagine replaced by lysine at position B3 and lysine replaced by glutamic acid at position B29) reduce the tendency to form hexamers, so glulisine dissociates and is absorbed more rapidly than regular human insulin, producing a faster onset and shorter duration of glucose-lowering action that mimics physiologic mealtime insulin secretion.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to insulin glulisine or any of its excipients
relative: Conditions or drugs causing hypokalemia (insulin shifts potassium intracellularly)
Renal or hepatic impairment (insulin requirements may fall - intensify monitoring)
Changes in physical activity, meal pattern, or concomitant medications altering glucose
monitor: Blood glucose, especially with dose changes or changes in routine
Serum potassium in patients at risk for hypokalemia

preg: Poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy increases maternal risk for diabetic ketoacidosis, infections, and preeclampsia, and fetal/neonatal risks including major birth defects, macrosomia, and hypoglycemia. Insulin is generally the preferred agent for managing diabetes during pregnancy. Insulin requirements typically fall in the first trimester and rise in the second and third trimesters and immediately postpartum; dose adjustment with close glucose monitoring is required.
lact: Endogenous insulin is present in human milk; exogenous insulin glulisine, a protein, is expected to be degraded in the infant's gastrointestinal tract and is not anticipated to cause harm to a breastfed infant. Breastfeeding women may require adjustments in insulin dose and diet.
renal: Some studies with human insulins have shown increased circulating insulin levels in patients with renal impairment. As with all insulins, glulisine requirements may be reduced in patients with renal impairment. Careful glucose monitoring and dose adjustment may be necessary; no specific dose reduction is defined.
hepatic: Insulin requirements may be diminished in patients with hepatic impairment due to reduced capacity for gluconeogenesis and reduced insulin metabolism. Frequent glucose monitoring and individualized dose adjustment are recommended; no specific fixed adjustment is defined.

major: Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) with insulin - increased risk of fluid retention and heart failure; monitor for signs of heart failure
moderate: Drugs that may increase the glucose-lowering effect and hypoglycemia risk: oral antidiabetics, ACE inhibitors, disopyramide, fibrates, fluoxetine, MAO inhibitors, pentoxifylline, propoxyphene, salicylates, somatostatin analogs (octreotide), sulfonamide antibiotics

Drugs that may reduce the glucose-lowering effect (hyperglycemia): corticosteroids, niacin, danazol, diuretics, sympathomimetics (epinephrine, albuterol, terbutaline), glucagon, isoniazid, phenothiazines, somatropin, thyroid hormones, estrogens/progestogens, protease inhibitors, atypical antipsychotics
Beta-blockers, clonidine, lithium, alcohol - may either potentiate or weaken the glucose-lowering effect
Pentamidine - may cause hypoglycemia, sometimes followed by hyperglycemia
minor: Beta-blockers, clonidine, guanethidine, and reserpine may blunt the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia
interactions.food: Designed to be given with meals; timing relative to food is integral to its use. Adjust dose for changes in carbohydrate intake or meal patterns.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may increase or decrease the blood-glucose-lowering effect of insulin and can mask hypoglycemia symptoms; counsel patients and monitor glucose.
interactions.diagnostics: Insulin lowers serum potassium; monitor potassium in at-risk patients. No characteristic laboratory assay interference, but glucose monitoring is central to dosing.

serious: Severe hypoglycemia (may cause seizures, loss of consciousness, death)
Hypokalemia (may cause respiratory paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia, death)
Heart failure when used with thiazolidinediones
rare: Cutaneous amyloidosis at repeated injection sites
emergency: Severe hypoglycemia with seizures or loss of consciousness
Severe hypokalemia with arrhythmia or respiratory compromise
Diabetic ketoacidosis from pump malfunction or insulin omission

monitoring: Blood glucose - frequent self-monitoring, especially with dose or regimen changes
HbA1c periodically to assess long-term control
Serum potassium in patients at risk for hypokalemia
Signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia and hypoglycemia unawareness
Injection sites for lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis
Body weight and signs of fluid retention/heart failure (if combined with a thiazolidinedione)
counsel: Inject this insulin within 15 minutes before your meal or within 20 minutes after you start eating
It works fast and does not last long, so always eat after you take it to avoid low blood sugar
Use it together with your long-acting (basal) insulin unless you use an insulin pump
Know the signs of low blood sugar - shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, confusion - and treat it quickly with sugar
Rotate your injection sites and check them; do not inject into lumps or pitted skin
Never share your pen, cartridge, or needle with anyone, even if you change the needle
Check your blood sugar more often when you are sick, change your meals, exercise more, or drink alcohol
If you use a pump, change the reservoir and tubing at least every 48 hours and watch for high sugar that may signal a pump problem
pk: Plasma peak around 60 minutes; glucose-lowering peak effect ~1 hour
About 13 minutes after subcutaneous administration (5-6 minutes IV)
Approximately 3-5 hours (shorter than regular human insulin)
Unopened: refrigerate 2-8 C, do not freeze. In use: room temperature below 25 C, vial up to 28 days, pen 28 days; protect from heat and light
pearls: Faster onset and shorter duration than regular insulin - excellent for mealtime/bolus coverage and post-meal dosing flexibility
Can be given within 20 minutes AFTER starting a meal, useful in patients with unpredictable intake (e.g., children)
Must be paired with a basal insulin for subcutaneous regimens; alone it does not provide background coverage
Pump-compatible but do not dilute or mix in the pump; change reservoir and set at least every 48 hours
If mixed in a syringe, only mix with NPH and draw glulisine first; inject immediately
Approved for pediatric patients aged 4 years and older
Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly - watch potassium in at-risk patients
missed: Insulin glulisine is dosed with meals, so there is no fixed schedule to make up. If you forget a dose and have already eaten, check your blood sugar and contact your healthcare provider for guidance rather than taking a large catch-up dose. Do not double doses. Never inject extra insulin to compensate without checking your blood glucose first.
overdose: Excess insulin relative to food intake, energy expenditure, or both causes hypoglycemia and may cause hypokalemia. Mild hypoglycemia can be treated with oral glucose/carbohydrate. Severe hypoglycemia with coma, seizure, or neurologic impairment requires intramuscular/subcutaneous glucagon or intravenous concentrated glucose, followed by carbohydrate intake and observation, since hypoglycemia may recur after apparent recovery. Monitor and correct potassium.
